I. The Historical Precedent: Noncitizen Voting Is an American Tradition

One of the most persistent misconceptions in American political discourse is the assumption that restricting the vote to citizens is a timeless, foundational feature of the republic. In fact, for the majority of American history, noncitizens voted regularly and legally. From 1776 through the early twentieth century, at least forty states and territories permitted noncitizens—often described as "declarant aliens" who had declared their intent to become citizens—to vote in local, state, and even federal elections. The practice was not marginal or accidental. It was a deliberate policy choice, embraced by lawmakers across the political spectrum, designed to integrate newcomers into democratic life and to ensure that the communities they helped build reflected their interests and needs.

Arkansas permitted noncitizen voting until 1926. Texas maintained the practice until 1921. In the Midwest, states like Wisconsin, Minnesota, Indiana, and Kansas extended the franchise to noncitizens for decades. The erosion of noncitizen voting rights was not the result of a principled constitutional reckoning; rather, it was driven by waves of nativist sentiment, particularly anti-German hostility during World War I and broader xenophobic anxieties during periods of mass immigration. The restriction was born not of democratic theory but of prejudice and exclusion—the same impulses that previously denied the vote to women, Black Americans, Indigenous peoples, and those without property.

Recognizing this history matters because it dismantles the myth that citizen-only voting is an immutable norm. The question is not whether America can extend the franchise to noncitizens—it already did so, for over a century—but whether it should do so again. History suggests that when the nation expanded voting rights, democracy grew stronger, not weaker.

II. The Democratic Philosophical Foundation: Consent of the Governed

The philosophical case for noncitizen voting is rooted in the deepest commitments of democratic theory. Democracy, at its most essential, is the principle that people who are subject to laws should have a meaningful say in making those laws. This principle—what political theorists call the "all-affected interests" principle—does not hinge on the possession of a particular legal document. It hinges on the reality of being governed.

Legal permanent residents and long-term noncitizen residents are governed by American laws in every conceivable way. They must obey criminal statutes. They pay federal, state, and local taxes—income taxes, property taxes, sales taxes, Social Security and Medicare taxes. They are subject to zoning regulations, environmental rules, labor laws, public health mandates, and the full apparatus of government authority. Their children attend public schools shaped by school board decisions. Their neighborhoods are policed by officers accountable to elected officials. Their water is cleaned—or not—according to policies set by elected representatives. Their wages are affected by minimum wage laws, trade policies, and economic regulations decided by legislators for whom they cannot vote.

John Locke, whose philosophy profoundly influenced the American founders, argued that legitimate government rests on the consent of the governed. The Declaration of Independence enshrined this ideal, proclaiming that governments derive "their just powers from the consent of the governed"—not the consent of citizens alone. The governed, in the American context, include every person who lives under the jurisdiction of American law. When millions of those people are denied any mechanism for expressing consent or dissent through the ballot box, the government's democratic legitimacy is compromised.

Consider the philosophical alternative: if we accept that only citizens deserve political representation, we must accept that it is just and proper for a democratic government to exercise coercive power over millions of people who have no recourse, no voice, and no means of holding their rulers accountable. This is precisely the arrangement the American Revolution was fought to reject.

III. Taxation Without Representation: The Economic Argument

The economic contributions of noncitizen residents make their political exclusion especially indefensible. Legal permanent residents alone number approximately 13.6 million people in the United States. When combined with other categories of long-term noncitizen residents—those on extended work visas, recipients of Temporary Protected Status, DACA beneficiaries, and others—the number of people who contribute economically while being denied political voice grows substantially larger.

These residents pay an estimated tens of billions of dollars in federal taxes annually, along with billions more in state and local taxes. The Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy has documented that undocumented immigrants alone pay approximately $11.7 billion per year in state and local taxes; legal permanent residents and authorized long-term residents contribute far more. These tax dollars fund schools, roads, emergency services, military operations, Social Security, and Medicare—programs and institutions whose direction is determined by elected officials for whom these taxpayers cannot vote.

The American Revolution was fought, in part, over the principle that taxation without representation is tyranny. The colonists were not arguing that taxation itself was unjust; they were arguing that being taxed by a government in which they had no voice was a fundamental violation of their rights. Today, the United States imposes precisely this arrangement on millions of its residents. Legal permanent residents fund the government at the same rates as their citizen neighbors, yet they are categorically excluded from shaping how that government spends their money, sets their tax rates, or determines their priorities.

Some will respond that noncitizens can avoid this dilemma by naturalizing. But this response is inadequate for several reasons. The naturalization process is lengthy—often taking years or even decades—expensive, bureaucratically complex, and not equally accessible to all. Many legal permanent residents face language barriers, processing backlogs, or financial obstacles that delay or prevent naturalization through no fault of their own. Others may be unable to renounce their original citizenship due to family obligations, inheritance laws, or personal ties to their countries of origin. The existence of a pathway to citizenship does not justify years or decades of political voicelessness for people who are otherwise full participants in American economic and social life.

IV. The Representation Gap: How Exclusion Distorts Democracy

The exclusion of noncitizen residents from voting does not simply affect those individuals—it distorts the democratic process for entire communities. Areas with large noncitizen populations suffer from a representation gap: elected officials in these areas represent communities whose needs and preferences are only partially expressed through the electorate. When a significant portion of a district's residents cannot vote, the political incentives for elected officials shift. Politicians are responsive to voters; residents who cannot vote can be safely ignored, their concerns deprioritized, their neighborhoods underfunded.

This dynamic has tangible consequences. Research has shown that communities with large noncitizen populations receive less public investment, fewer government services, and less political attention than comparable communities where a higher proportion of residents can vote. Schools in these areas may be underfunded. Infrastructure may be neglected. Public safety resources may be inadequately allocated. The result is a two-tiered system of governance in which some residents matter politically and others do not—a system fundamentally at odds with the Equal Protection principles embedded in the Fourteenth Amendment, which guarantees equal protection of the laws to all persons, not merely to all citizens.

Moreover, the exclusion of noncitizen residents from voting weakens the political power of the citizen voters in those same communities. In heavily immigrant neighborhoods, citizen voters find their collective political voice diluted—not because too many people are voting, but because too few are. When only a fraction of a community's adult residents can participate in elections, that community's ability to advocate effectively for its interests is diminished relative to communities where nearly all residents can vote. Noncitizen enfranchisement would strengthen the democratic voice of these communities as a whole, ensuring that elected representatives are accountable to the full range of people they serve.

V. Integration and Civic Belonging: Voting as a Pathway to Inclusion

One of the strongest pragmatic arguments for noncitizen voting is its potential to promote civic integration. Voting is not merely a mechanism for selecting leaders; it is an act of civic participation that connects individuals to their communities and fosters a sense of belonging and investment. When we tell long-term residents that they are welcome to work, pay taxes, and raise families in the United States but are not welcome to participate in the most fundamental act of democratic citizenship, we send a powerful message of exclusion. We create a permanent underclass of residents who are economically integrated but politically marginalized.

Research from countries and municipalities that have extended voting rights to noncitizens supports the conclusion that enfranchisement promotes integration. In countries like New Zealand, which grants voting rights to permanent residents, and in European nations that permit noncitizen voting in local elections, studies have found that the extension of the franchise encourages civic engagement beyond voting itself—including volunteerism, community organizing, and participation in public institutions.

In the United States, several municipalities have already taken steps in this direction. Takoma Park, Maryland, extended voting rights to noncitizen residents in local elections in 1992, and the sky did not fall. The policy has been widely regarded as successful, promoting engagement and inclusion without any of the catastrophic consequences opponents predicted. More recently, municipalities in Vermont, and jurisdictions including San Francisco and New York City, have debated or implemented limited noncitizen voting provisions. These experiments provide valuable evidence that noncitizen enfranchisement is workable, manageable, and beneficial.

Extending voting rights to long-term noncitizen residents would also reduce the alienation and disenfranchisement that can fuel social division. When people feel that they have a stake in the system—that their voices are heard and their participation is valued—they are more likely to invest in the health and stability of their communities. Conversely, when people are systematically excluded from political life, the resulting frustration and marginalization can undermine social cohesion. Enfranchisement is not just a right; it is a tool for building a more unified and resilient democracy.

VI. Answering the Objections

No serious argument for noncitizen voting can ignore the objections that will be raised against it. These objections deserve respectful engagement—and, ultimately, rejection.

"Voting is a privilege of citizenship."

This is the most common objection, and it rests on a circular logic: voting should be restricted to citizens because voting is a right of citizenship. But this merely restates the current arrangement without justifying it. The question is why voting should be restricted to citizens, and the answer cannot simply be "because it currently is." Throughout American history, the boundaries of the franchise have been redrawn repeatedly—expanding to include nonpropertied men, Black men, women, and eighteen-year-olds. Each expansion was opposed by those who insisted that voting was a privilege belonging only to those who already had it. Each expansion made democracy stronger and more legitimate. Restricting the vote to citizens is a policy choice, not a natural law, and like all policy choices, it should be evaluated on its merits.

Furthermore, citizenship already confers numerous privileges that would remain unique to citizens even if voting rights were extended: the right to hold federal office, the right to serve on federal juries, immunity from deportation, the right to a U.S. passport, and access to certain government programs. Voting is important, but it need not be the singular marker that distinguishes citizens from noncitizens.

"Noncitizens lack sufficient attachment to the country."

This objection is empirically unfounded. Legal permanent residents have, by definition, established long-term ties to the United States. Many have lived in the country for decades. They own homes, run businesses, serve in the armed forces, and raise American-citizen children. To suggest that a person who has lived in the United States for ten, twenty, or thirty years—paying taxes, contributing to the economy, and raising a family—lacks sufficient attachment to the country is to privilege a piece of paper over the lived reality of belonging.

Moreover, the attachment argument proves too much. We do not require citizens to demonstrate attachment, knowledge, or investment before they vote. A citizen who has never paid taxes, never volunteered, never read a newspaper, and has no understanding of public policy can vote without restriction. If attachment is the criterion, then it should be applied consistently—or not at all.

"Noncitizen voting would dilute the votes of citizens."

This objection reflects a zero-sum understanding of democracy that is both philosophically impoverished and empirically incorrect. Democracy is not a finite resource that is diminished when more people participate. The inclusion of women in the electorate did not dilute the votes of men; it enriched and legitimized the democratic process. The same is true of every expansion of the franchise. More participation means more representation, more accountability, and a more accurate reflection of the community's will.

"Noncitizens might vote in ways that harm the national interest."

This objection is rooted in suspicion rather than evidence, and it echoes the same fears that were once deployed against Catholic voters, immigrant voters, Black voters, and women voters. Every group that has been denied the vote has been characterized as untrustworthy, ignorant, or dangerous. In every case, these fears proved unfounded. Noncitizen residents share the same fundamental interests as their citizen neighbors: safe communities, good schools, functioning infrastructure, a healthy economy, and responsive government. There is no reason to assume that their political preferences would be harmful, and significant reason to believe that their participation would make governance more responsive and representative.

"The Constitution restricts voting to citizens."

This objection requires careful examination. The Constitution does not explicitly grant the right to vote to citizens only—at least not in all elections. The Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments use the word "citizens" in the context of certain voting protections, but they do not prohibit extending the franchise to noncitizens. The Constitution leaves the regulation of elections primarily to the states, and there is a strong legal argument that states and municipalities have the authority to extend voting rights to noncitizen residents in state and local elections. At the federal level, a constitutional amendment might be required—but constitutional amendments are precisely the mechanism by which the nation has historically expanded the franchise when justice demanded it.

VII. A Vision for a More Perfect Union

The United States has always been a nation in the process of becoming. Its history is a story of progressive—if painfully slow—expansion of rights and recognition, of the gradual closing of the gap between the nation's ideals and its practices. The preamble to the Constitution aspires to "form a more perfect Union," an acknowledgment that perfection is a goal to be pursued, not a state already achieved.

Extending voting rights to legal permanent residents and long-term noncitizen residents is the next natural step in this ongoing project. It is consistent with the nation's founding philosophy, supported by its own historical practice, demanded by basic principles of fairness and representation, and beneficial to the strength and cohesion of its communities. It would bring millions of people out of political invisibility, ensure that elected officials are accountable to the full range of people they govern, promote civic integration, and strengthen the democratic legitimacy of a government that currently exercises power over millions who have no say in how that power is used.

The question is not whether noncitizen residents deserve a voice in the democracy that shapes their lives. By every principle the United States claims to hold dear—consent of the governed, equal protection under law, no taxation without representation, government of, by, and for the people—they do. The question is whether the United States has the courage, the moral clarity, and the democratic conviction to recognize what justice requires.

The answer should be yes. It always should have been yes.

The arc of American democracy bends toward inclusion—but only when citizens demand that it does. It is time to extend the franchise once more, to welcome into the democratic process the millions of residents who have already given their labor, their taxes, their talents, and their futures to this country. They have earned the right to be heard. A nation that believes in democracy should let them speak.

The Unfinished Promise: Why Long-Term Residents Deserve a Voice

Friends, neighbors, fellow believers in democracy—

They stock the same grocery shelves, staff the same hospitals, patrol the same fire stations, and mourn at the same funerals. They pay every single tax—federal, state, local, property, sales—that their citizen neighbors pay.

And yet, when the decisions are made about how those tax dollars are spent, when school boards are elected, when city councils vote on zoning that reshapes their neighborhoods, when Congress decides whether to send their children to war—they are told to be silent.

Let me ask you something that should unsettle every one of us: What do we call a system where people are governed without their consent? Where people are taxed without representation?

We already answered that question once. In 1776.

I. The Historical Truth They Don't Want You to Remember

The advocates of the status quo will tell you that voting has always been exclusively for citizens. That is simply, factually, historically wrong.

For much of American history—from the founding era until the early twentieth century—non-citizens voted in at least forty states and territories. They voted in local elections, state elections, and even federal elections. The Constitution itself never restricted voting to citizens. The Framers left that power to the states, and state after state chose to enfranchise those who had planted their lives in American soil.

It was not some radical experiment. It was the norm. It was understood that people who lived in a community, contributed to a community, and bore the burdens of a community had a fundamental right to participate in governing that community.

The restriction of voting to citizens alone came later—driven not by democratic principle but by nativism, xenophobia, and the ugly politics of exclusion. It came in the same era that saw literacy tests, poll taxes, and systematic disenfranchisement of Black Americans. It was part of the same poisoned project: narrowing the electorate to maintain the power of the few.

We have spent a century tearing down those other barriers. It is time to confront this one.

II. Taxation Without Representation Is Still Tyranny

Let me put real numbers to this injustice.

Long-term noncitizen residents contribute an estimated $30 billion or more in federal taxes every single year, along with billions more in state and local taxes. They fund the roads they drive on, the schools their children attend, the police departments that protect them, and the military that defends them.

In return, they get no voice. None.

Imagine—really imagine—that tomorrow, the government told you that you would keep paying every tax, keep obeying every law, keep facing every consequence of government action—but you could never again cast a vote. Not for president, not for governor, not for your local school board. You would still be fined if you broke a law you had no part in making. You would still be sent to war if Congress declared one. But the ballot box? Closed to you. Forever—or at least for years, possibly a decade or more.

Would you accept that?

Then why—why—do we accept it for our neighbors?

III. The Citizenship Argument and Why It Falls Short

Now, I know what some of you are thinking. You're thinking: "They can become citizens. The path is there. If they want to vote, they should naturalize."

I hear you. And I want to engage with that argument honestly, because it deserves honesty.

First: the naturalization process is not the simple, accessible path that many Americans imagine. It takes a minimum of five years of permanent residency—often much longer. It costs over $700 in fees alone, not counting legal assistance that many applicants need. It requires navigating a bureaucracy so backlogged that wait times stretch for years. For some, there are language barriers, literacy challenges, or disabilities that make the civics test a genuine obstacle—even though their investment in this country is beyond question.

And for some, there are deeply personal reasons—ties to a homeland, family obligations, cultural identity—that make renouncing allegiance to another country a wrenching choice. Must we demand that people sever part of who they are before we let them participate in the community they already belong to?

But here's the deeper point: even if the path to citizenship were faster, easier, and cheaper—even if every barrier were removed—the argument would still miss the mark.

Because the question is not, "Can they eventually earn this right?" The question is, "Is it just to deny it to them now?"

A person who has lived in this country for five, ten, fifteen years, who has built a business, raised a family, buried a loved one in American soil—that person is already a member of this community. Their membership is not theoretical. It is not pending. It is real and present and daily. And democracy means that the people who are affected by decisions get to participate in making them. Not someday. Now.

IV. Democracy Means ALL Who Are Governed

Let me offer you a principle, and I want you to test it against your conscience:

The legitimacy of democratic government rests on the consent of the governed.

Not the consent of some of the governed. Not the consent of the governed who were born in the right place. All of the governed.

When thirteen million people—people who are here lawfully, who have been vetted, who have been invited by this nation to make their lives here—are excluded from the political process, we do not have a complete democracy. We have a selective one. And a selective democracy is a weakened one.

Think about what that exclusion means in practice. In some communities, noncitizen residents make up twenty, thirty, even forty percent of the adult population. That means elected officials in those communities can effectively ignore the needs of a third or more of the people they supposedly serve. Why would a city council member fight for better labor protections in a neighborhood where half the workers can't vote? Why would a school board member prioritize a school where most parents have no political power?

This isn't hypothetical. This is happening right now, in cities and towns across America. The voiceless are overlooked. The powerless are underserved. And we dress it up in the language of citizenship and pretend it's principled.

V. Stronger Communities, Not Weaker Ones

Let me speak now to the fear—because I know it's there, and I refuse to pretend it isn't.

Some fear that extending voting rights to noncitizens will somehow dilute the meaning of citizenship, weaken national identity, or open the door to chaos.

I want to challenge that fear with evidence and with vision.

The evidence: Countries around the world—New Zealand, many European Union nations, parts of Canada and South America—allow noncitizen residents to vote in various elections. The result has not been chaos. It has been greater civic integration, higher levels of community trust, and stronger social cohesion. When people are invited to participate, they invest more deeply. They learn more about their communities. They become better neighbors, not worse ones.

The vision: A community where everyone who lives there has a stake, has a voice, and has a reason to show up—not just to work and pay taxes, but to shape the future. Imagine a PTA where every parent can vote for the school board. Imagine a neighborhood association where every resident can vote for the city council. Imagine the dignity—the simple, profound dignity—of being told: "You matter here. Your voice counts."

Inclusion does not weaken a community. Exclusion does.

When we shut people out, we don't protect democracy. We create an underclass. We create resentment. We create neighborhoods where half the residents feel like they don't belong—because we have told them they don't.

And let me say this plainly: there is nothing more dangerous to a democracy than a large, permanent population of people who live under its laws but have no power to change them. That is not stability. That is a pressure cooker.

VI. A Practical Path Forward

I am not standing here asking for something reckless. I am asking for something reasonable.

We can begin where it makes the most sense: local elections. School boards, city councils, municipal ballot measures. The decisions that most directly and immediately affect daily life. Several municipalities have already taken this step—in Maryland, in Vermont, in parts of California and New York. The sky has not fallen.

We can establish clear criteria: lawful residency of a defined duration. Two years, three years—a period that demonstrates commitment and rootedness. We can include permanent residents, those with long-term work or family visas, refugees, and asylees who have been granted protection by this nation and are building their lives within it.

We can expand from there, as confidence grows and as the evidence mounts—because it will mount—that broader participation makes for better governance.

And for those who say this requires a constitutional amendment—let's be clear about the law. The Constitution does not prohibit noncitizen voting. It has been read to leave that power with the states, just as it did for the first hundred-plus years of this republic. States and localities have the authority to act. What they need is the political will. And political will comes from movements, from voices, from people like us demanding better.

VII. The Moral Core

Let me close with what I believe is the heart of this matter.

Every major expansion of the franchise in American history was opposed by people who said it would go too far. They said it when we proposed ending property requirements. They said it when we fought for the Fifteenth Amendment. They said it when women demanded the Nineteenth. They said it when eighteen-year-olds—old enough to die in Vietnam but not to vote—were finally enfranchised by the Twenty-Sixth.
